chunks.text: In Bangladesh the government provides family-planning information and contraceptives **free** through the Directorate General of Family Planning (DGFP). Field workers (family welfare assistants) and Union and Upazila family-planning offices bring services close to where women live. A woman can get counselling to choose the method that suits her, and services are confidential.
chunks.title: Family planning services in Bangladesh
chunks.source: DGFP — Directorate General of Family Planning, Bangladesh

chunks.text: The national program offers a range of methods: the combined oral contraceptive pill (the national brand is called "Sukhi"), progestogen-only pills, injectable contraceptives, intrauterine devices (IUDs), implants, condoms, emergency contraception, and permanent methods (female or male sterilisation) for those who have completed their family. Which method is safe depends on a woman's health, so it is best chosen with a health worker.
chunks.title: Family planning services in Bangladesh
chunks.source: DGFP — Directorate General of Family Planning, Bangladesh

chunks.text: The program gives special attention to family planning right after childbirth (postpartum family planning), which helps a mother space her pregnancies safely. About 12% of married women in Bangladesh still have an unmet need for family planning. To start, a woman can visit her nearest community clinic, union health & family welfare centre, or upazila health complex, or call the government health hotline Shastho Batayon on 16263 — the guidance is free and non-judgmental.
chunks.title: Family planning services in Bangladesh
chunks.source: DGFP — Directorate General of Family Planning, Bangladesh
chunks.section: After childbirth, and where to ask

chunks.text: In Bangladesh, menstrual regulation (MR) is a government-provided service to bring back menstruation and return a woman to a non-pregnant state after a missed period. It is offered through the Directorate General of Family Planning (DGFP). Depending on the method and provider, MR is generally available up to about 10–12 weeks after the last menstrual period; the medication method (MRM, using mifepristone and misoprostol) is used up to about 9 weeks.
chunks.title: Menstrual regulation and post-abortion care in Bangladesh

chunks.text: MR should be done by a trained provider at a recognised government or approved facility — not with unknown pills bought without advice, which can be unsafe. Trained providers use safe methods (manual vacuum aspiration or approved medication) and can advise on what is right for the woman's situation. After MR, it is important to start a family-planning method to avoid another unintended pregnancy, and services can provide this counselling.
chunks.title: Menstrual regulation and post-abortion care in Bangladesh

chunks.text: If a woman has heavy bleeding, severe pain, fever, or bad-smelling discharge after a miscarriage or MR, she should seek care immediately — post-abortion care is available at DGHS facilities and can treat complications. In an emergency call 999; for free, confidential advice call the health hotline Shastho Batayon on 16263. The guidance here is general information, not a substitute for seeing a trained health provider.
chunks.title: Menstrual regulation and post-abortion care in Bangladesh
chunks.section: Post-abortion care and when to seek help

chunks.text: Antenatal care (ANC) means the health check-ups a woman should have during pregnancy. Bangladesh's national schedule recommends at least four ANC visits: the first before about 16 weeks, the second between 24 and 28 weeks, the third around 32 weeks, and the fourth around 36 weeks. WHO now recommends at least eight contacts for the best care. Starting early and going to every visit helps keep the mother and baby safe.
chunks.title: Antenatal (pregnancy) care in Bangladesh
chunks.source: DGHS/DGFP Bangladesh national schedule & WHO antenatal care recommendations

chunks.text: At each visit a health worker checks blood pressure, weight and (when needed) blood and urine; gives the tetanus (TT/Td) vaccine and iron–folic acid tablets to prevent anaemia; and answers questions. These services are available free at government facilities — community clinics, union health & family welfare centres, and upazila health complexes.
chunks.title: Antenatal (pregnancy) care in Bangladesh
chunks.source: DGHS/DGFP Bangladesh national schedule & WHO antenatal care recommendations
chunks.section: What happens at a visit, and where

chunks.text: During pregnancy, seek care immediately for: vaginal bleeding, severe headache, blurred vision, swelling of the face or hands, convulsions (fits), high fever, or the baby moving much less than usual. In an emergency call 999; for free health advice call the government health hotline Shastho Batayon 16263.
chunks.title: Antenatal (pregnancy) care in Bangladesh
chunks.source: DGHS/DGFP Bangladesh national schedule & WHO antenatal care recommendations
chunks.section: Danger signs — go to a facility at once

chunks.text: Bleeding after childbirth (postpartum haemorrhage) is a leading cause of maternal death. icddr,b research showed that giving the medicine misoprostol through clean delivery kits protected about 60% of home births in the project from postpartum haemorrhage — evidence that has helped shape safer delivery practice in Bangladesh. A skilled birth attendant and delivering at a facility make birth safer for mother and baby.
chunks.title: Maternal and newborn health in Bangladesh (icddr,b evidence)
chunks.source: icddr,b — Maternal and neonatal health research

chunks.text: Since the late 1970s, icddr,b pioneered a model using large numbers of trained female community health workers to bring family planning and maternal care to women's doorsteps. This dramatically increased contraceptive use and lowered fertility, and the approach is now used widely across Bangladesh — showing that trusted local workers can reach rural women who cannot easily travel.
chunks.title: Maternal and newborn health in Bangladesh (icddr,b evidence)
chunks.source: icddr,b — Maternal and neonatal health research
chunks.section: Community health workers reach women at home

chunks.text: icddr,b worked with adolescents to build a bank of reproductive-health questions and answers, used to update a Bangla reproductive-health booklet series called "Nijeke Jano" ("Know Yourself"). Giving young people clear, non-judgmental, science-based answers in Bangla helps counter myths and shame. This is general information; a woman or girl with a health concern should also speak with a doctor or health worker.
chunks.title: Maternal and newborn health in Bangladesh (icddr,b evidence)
chunks.source: icddr,b — Maternal and neonatal health research

chunks.text: Menopause is when periods stop for good because hormone levels fall; perimenopause is the time before, when symptoms have started but periods have not yet fully stopped. They are a natural part of life and usually affect women between the ages of 45 and 55, though they can happen earlier.
chunks.title: Menopause and perimenopause

chunks.text: Periods often become irregular before stopping. Many women get hot flushes and night sweats — a sudden feeling of heat in the face, neck and chest, sometimes with sweating, palpitations or dizziness lasting a few minutes. Mental-health symptoms are common too: mood swings, low mood or anxiety, and problems with memory or concentration ("brain fog"), often made worse by poor sleep. Physical symptoms can include vaginal dryness and discomfort during sex, reduced sex drive, more frequent urinary infections and needing to pass urine more often, palpitations, headaches, joint and muscle aches, and changes to skin and hair.
chunks.title: Menopause and perimenopause

chunks.text: Contact a doctor if you think you have perimenopause or menopause symptoms, especially if your bleeding pattern changes a lot, or if you have any vaginal bleeding after 12 months without a period. Treatments and self-care can reduce the impact on health, relationships and work.
chunks.title: Menopause and perimenopause

chunks.text:
UNICEF Bangladesh highlights the importance of adolescent health services, education, life skills, digital literacy, nutrition, and girls' participation in decisions that affect them. Young people should be treated with respect and given safe, age-appropriate information.

Child marriage and violence can interrupt education, limit choices, and create health risks. Prevention requires trusted adults, communities, services, and the meaningful participation of girls. A girl facing pressure or harm should be supported without blame and connected to safe help.
chunks.title: Adolescent girls and children in Bangladesh

chunks.text: Good nutrition supports growth, learning, immunity, pregnancy, recovery, and daily energy. Families can choose a varied diet using foods available locally, such as vegetables, fruits, pulses, eggs, fish, or meat. Food needs vary by age, pregnancy, illness, and household resources, so local health advice matters.
chunks.title: UNICEF Bangladesh health, nutrition, WASH, and climate resilience

chunks.text:
Anaemia and other nutrient deficiencies can affect children, adolescents, pregnant women, and mothers. Ongoing tiredness, weakness, dizziness, or breathlessness should be discussed with a qualified health worker because several conditions can cause these symptoms. Do not start high-dose supplements without advice.

Pregnancy increases the importance of regular antenatal care and practical nutrition support. A health worker can advise on local foods, prescribed supplements, and warning signs. Shokhi can help prepare questions, but it should not prescribe a dose or replace antenatal assessment.
chunks.title: UNICEF Bangladesh health, nutrition, WASH, and climate resilience

chunks.text:
Adolescence is a period of rapid growth. Girls need enough food, rest, and support to learn and stay healthy. Menstrual blood loss, food insecurity, infections, and other health concerns can affect energy. Persistent weakness or dizziness deserves a health-worker discussion rather than blame.

Families should follow local government and health guidance about water safety, especially after flooding, salinity, pipe damage, or other disruption. Use a safer source or treatment method recommended locally. If several people become ill after using water, seek public-health or medical advice.
chunks.title: UNICEF Bangladesh health, nutrition, WASH, and climate resilience

chunks.text:
Handwashing with soap or an appropriate local alternative at key times helps reduce the spread of infection. Children need facilities they can reach and understand. Water points should be safe, accessible, and usable by people with disabilities.

Girls and women need privacy, clean absorbent materials, water, soap, and a safe place to change or wash. Schools, workplaces, shelters, and homes should plan for disposal or washing. Menstruation is normal; teasing, exclusion, and forcing someone to use unsafe materials are harmful.
chunks.title: UNICEF Bangladesh health, nutrition, WASH, and climate resilience

chunks.text:
Schools need toilets that are private, safe, accessible, and usable during menstruation. Reliable water and handwashing support health and attendance. A student who cannot access a toilet safely should be able to tell a trusted teacher or school manager without shame.

Floods, cyclones, salinity, and damaged water points can interrupt food, medicines, menstrual supplies, schooling, and health care. Families can keep a small emergency kit, protect important documents, follow official warnings, and plan how to reach a safe place. Local disaster guidance takes priority.
chunks.title: UNICEF Bangladesh health, nutrition, WASH, and climate resilience

chunks.text: Children, pregnant women, older people, and people with health conditions may be more vulnerable in extreme heat. Follow local alerts, rest in a cooler place, drink safe water, wear light clothing, and avoid the hottest hours when possible. New severe symptoms need medical attention.
chunks.title: UNICEF Bangladesh health, nutrition, WASH, and climate resilience

chunks.text:
Health services and schools need plans for heat, floods, cyclones, and disease risks. Families should check whether a clinic, pharmacy, school, or water point has moved or changed hours after a disaster. Do not assume a service is operating normally during an emergency.

Displacement, loss, fear, interrupted school, and family stress can affect mood and sleep. Listening, routine, play, supportive adults, and connection with services can help. Persistent distress, inability to function, self-harm thoughts, or immediate danger need prompt professional support.
chunks.title: UNICEF Bangladesh health, nutrition, WASH, and climate resilience

chunks.text:
After a disaster, follow local advice about safe food and water. Avoid food that is spoiled, contaminated, or stored unsafely. Infants, pregnant people, older adults, and people with chronic conditions may need extra support to maintain safe nutrition.

An emergency kit can include essential medicines prescribed for the family, menstrual materials, safe water, food, a torch, phone charging support, and important documents. Medicines should be kept dry and used only as directed. Ask a health worker what to do if supplies are lost.
chunks.title: UNICEF Bangladesh health, nutrition, WASH, and climate resilience

chunks.text:
Emergency messages, shelters, toilets, water points, and health services should be accessible. Ask the person what communication or mobility support they prefer. Do not separate a person from their chosen support person unless safety procedures require it.

Severe pain, heavy bleeding, fainting, trouble breathing, confusion, convulsions, severe dehydration, or danger to a child or pregnant person need urgent care. For less urgent concerns, contact a qualified health worker and explain the symptoms, timing, and any recent heatwave, flood, or water disruption.
chunks.title: UNICEF Bangladesh health, nutrition, WASH, and climate resilience

chunks.text: A girl or woman does not have to solve a difficult health or safety problem alone. A trusted family member, teacher, community health worker, social worker, or service provider can help her understand choices and reach care. Listening should be respectful and private where possible. No one should be blamed for asking a question or seeking help.
chunks.title: UNICEF Bangladesh services, protection, and participation

chunks.text:
Adolescents need age-appropriate information about their bodies, relationships, safety, nutrition, mental wellbeing, and services. Information should use simple words, allow questions, and respect the young person's privacy. A girl can ask a health worker to explain a service in a way she understands.

Poverty, disability, disasters, child labour, child marriage, and unsafe journeys can interrupt education. Families, schools, and communities can help girls continue learning by reducing barriers, offering practical support, and welcoming a safe return after absence. Education supports health, confidence, and future choices.
chunks.title: UNICEF Bangladesh services, protection, and participation

chunks.text: Digital learning can help children and adolescents reach information, but online spaces can also expose them to harassment, pressure, or harmful requests. Keep personal details private, use a trusted adult or teacher when something feels unsafe, and save evidence of serious threats if it is safe to do so. Immediate danger needs local emergency help.
chunks.title: UNICEF Bangladesh services, protection, and participation

chunks.text: Child marriage can limit education, choices, and access to health care, and can expose a girl to health and safety risks. Prevention should support girls' agency, education, families, and communities. A girl facing pressure should be supported without blame and connected with a trained protection or health service.
chunks.title: UNICEF Bangladesh services, protection, and participation

chunks.text: When a child or adolescent says someone harmed or threatened them, listen calmly, believe them, and avoid repeated questioning. Do not pressure them to confront an unsafe person. Help them reach a trained protection worker or another safe service. If there is immediate danger, move to safety and seek emergency help.
chunks.title: UNICEF Bangladesh services, protection, and participation
chunks.section: Responding when a child shares harm

chunks.text: Violence, coercion, harassment, and sexual abuse are never the survivor's fault. A person may need medical care, emotional support, protection planning, and confidential referral. Use a safe device and a trusted service when privacy is a concern. Shokhi should not investigate or promise secrecy it cannot guarantee.
chunks.title: UNICEF Bangladesh services, protection, and participation

chunks.text: A safe referral explains what kind of service may help, checks whether the person can reach it safely, and respects her decision. The helper should avoid sharing identifying details unnecessarily. If a child is involved, safeguarding procedures and trained local services should guide the next step.
chunks.title: UNICEF Bangladesh services, protection, and participation

chunks.text: Birth registration helps children establish legal identity and access services. Families who face barriers can ask a local government office, community worker, or child-protection service what documents and steps are needed. Shokhi can explain the general idea but should not invent local fees, deadlines, or document requirements.
chunks.title: UNICEF Bangladesh services, protection, and participation

chunks.text: Children and women with disabilities should be included in health care, education, social protection, and decisions about their own lives. A service may need an accessible entrance, plain language, sign support, communication assistance, extra time, or a companion chosen by the person. Ask what support the person prefers.
chunks.title: UNICEF Bangladesh services, protection, and participation

chunks.text:
Do not assume a disabled person cannot understand, decide, or speak for herself. Address her directly, ask before helping, and give information in an accessible format. Family support is valuable, but the person's preferences and privacy still matter.

Community health workers can connect families with antenatal care, immunisation, nutrition, family planning, protection, and other services. A worker may know which nearby facility provides a particular service. Shokhi should encourage users to confirm current opening times and availability locally.
chunks.title: UNICEF Bangladesh services, protection, and participation

chunks.text: Schools can be safe places to provide health information, emotional support, referrals, and practical help with menstruation or disability. A student who feels unsafe or is being bullied should be connected with a trusted teacher or safeguarding focal person, while protecting her privacy as much as possible.
chunks.title: UNICEF Bangladesh services, protection, and participation

chunks.text: Programs work better when girls and adolescents are listened to and included in decisions affecting them. Ask what she needs, what feels safe, and who she trusts. Do not treat participation as permission to expose private information or make a decision for her.
chunks.title: UNICEF Bangladesh services, protection, and participation

chunks.text: Families can support a girl by listening, helping her reach care, and respecting her choices. Pressure to marry, have sex, become pregnant, stop school, or hide violence is not health support. When family involvement could increase danger, seek confidential guidance from a trained service.
chunks.title: UNICEF Bangladesh services, protection, and participation

chunks.text: Immediate danger, severe injury, heavy bleeding, fainting, or thoughts of self-harm need urgent in-person help. For non-emergency concerns, a qualified health worker, social worker, school counsellor, or protection service can help plan the next step. This educational summary is not a substitute for local assessment.
chunks.title: UNICEF Bangladesh services, protection, and participation

chunks.text:
UNICEF-supported child protection community hubs in Bangladesh bring together families, schools, communities, and social workers. Their work includes preventing violence and child marriage, supporting birth registration, and helping children access safer services.

A child or adolescent who reports harm should be listened to, believed, and connected with trained support. Do not pressure the child to confront an unsafe person alone. Immediate danger requires emergency help and a safe place.
chunks.title: Community-based child protection in Bangladesh

chunks.text:
Children, pregnant women, older people, and people with health conditions can be vulnerable during heatwaves. Staying in a cooler place, drinking safe water, wearing light clothing, and avoiding the hottest hours can reduce risk.

Families can prepare safe water, food, medicines, menstrual supplies, a torch, and important documents before a disaster. Follow official warnings and move early to a safe place when instructed.
chunks.title: Climate and disaster safety for children in Bangladesh

chunks.text:
Children with disabilities should be visible, counted, and included in health care, education, recreation, social protection, and decisions about their lives. Services need coordination, accessibility, trained workers, and respect for the person's communication and preferences.

Families can ask services about reasonable accommodations such as accessible entrances, plain language, sign support, communication assistance, or extra time. Stigma, neglect, confinement, and violence are protection concerns.
chunks.title: Disability inclusion and services for children in Bangladesh

chunks.text:
UNICEF Bangladesh works toward education that is inclusive, relevant, accessible, and resilient during emergencies and climate disruption. Children who face poverty, disability, disaster, child labour, or child marriage may need extra support to stay in or return to learning.

Education for adolescents can include transferable life skills and alternative learning pathways for children who are out of school. Digital access should be paired with safety, inclusion, and support for children with limited connectivity.
chunks.title: Inclusive education and skills in Bangladesh

chunks.text:
Young people's mental wellbeing is supported by safe relationships, caring adults, inclusive schools, time to rest, and access to appropriate help. Listening without shame or blame makes it easier for a child or adolescent to ask for support.

Persistent distress, inability to function, self-harm thoughts, or immediate danger need prompt support from a qualified professional or emergency service. A young person in crisis should not be left alone.
chunks.title: Student mental health in Bangladesh

chunks.text:
UNICEF Bangladesh describes nutrition as important for growth, learning, immunity, and lifelong health. Families benefit from varied foods that may include vegetables, fruit, pulses, eggs, fish, or meat, according to availability and local advice.

Anaemia and micronutrient deficiencies affect children, adolescents, pregnant women, and mothers. Weakness, persistent tiredness, dizziness, or breathlessness should be discussed with a qualified health worker. Supplement decisions should follow local clinical guidance rather than self-treatment.
chunks.title: Nutrition for children, adolescents, and mothers in Bangladesh

chunks.text:
UNICEF Bangladesh notes that water quality, sanitation, handwashing, and climate-related disruption remain important concerns. Safe water decisions should follow local testing, government, and health guidance.

Girls and women need privacy, water, clean menstrual materials, and safe sanitation. Floods, salinity, and damaged water points can disrupt these services, so households and schools benefit from practical preparedness plans.
chunks.title: Water, sanitation, hygiene, and menstrual dignity in Bangladesh

chunks.text: WHO describes antenatal care as a platform for health promotion, screening, prevention, and support during pregnancy. The goal is not only to prevent complications but also to provide respectful, person-centred care and a positive pregnancy experience for pregnant women and adolescent girls.
chunks.title: WHO recommendations on antenatal care for a positive pregnancy experience
chunks.source: WHO — WHO recommendations on antenatal care for a positive pregnancy experience

chunks.text: Care is adapted by a qualified health worker and may include maternal and fetal assessment, nutrition counselling, prevention measures, support for common pregnancy symptoms, and discussion of emotional and social wellbeing. The timing and tests should follow local clinical guidance and the person's health needs.
chunks.title: WHO recommendations on antenatal care for a positive pregnancy experience
chunks.source: WHO — WHO recommendations on antenatal care for a positive pregnancy experience

chunks.text:
Shokhi can help a person prepare for an early antenatal visit, collect questions, record the first day of the last menstrual period, and remember to disclose medicines or existing conditions. It must not prescribe supplements, diagnose pregnancy complications, or replace an in-person assessment.

Bleeding, severe abdominal pain, severe headache, vision changes, sudden swelling, seizures, or reduced fetal movement require urgent clinical help. Shokhi's deterministic safety rules take priority over educational retrieval.
chunks.title: WHO recommendations on antenatal care for a positive pregnancy experience
chunks.source: WHO — WHO recommendations on antenatal care for a positive pregnancy experience
chunks.section: How Shokhi should use this source

chunks.text: The WHO Medical eligibility criteria for contraceptive use (MEC), sixth edition, gives evidence-based recommendations on the safety of different contraceptive methods for people who have specific health conditions or characteristics. Its purpose is to help health workers support a woman to choose and safely use a family-planning method.
chunks.title: Medical eligibility criteria for contraceptive use
chunks.source: WHO — Medical eligibility criteria for contraceptive use, 6th edition (2025)

chunks.text: For each medical condition, a method is placed into one of four categories. Categories 1 and 2 mean the woman can generally use the method (the benefits usually outweigh any risk). Categories 3 and 4 mean the method should generally not be used, because the risk usually outweighs the benefit. Safety considers whether a method could worsen a condition or add health risks, and whether a condition makes the method less effective — always weighed against the benefit of preventing an unintended pregnancy.
chunks.title: Medical eligibility criteria for contraceptive use
chunks.source: WHO — Medical eligibility criteria for contraceptive use, 6th edition (2025)

chunks.text: The guidance covers a wide range of methods, including low-dose combined oral contraceptives, the patch and vaginal ring, injectables (DMPA, NET-EN), progestogen-only pills, implants, emergency contraceptive pills, and copper and hormonal (levonorgestrel) intrauterine devices (IUDs). A woman should discuss her health history with a doctor or family-planning worker to find the method that is safe and right for her.
chunks.title: Medical eligibility criteria for contraceptive use
chunks.source: WHO — Medical eligibility criteria for contraceptive use, 6th edition (2025)

chunks.text: The Selected practice recommendations (SPR), fourth edition, explains how to start, continue and manage problems with contraceptive methods after a method is considered medically appropriate. It complements the WHO Medical eligibility criteria already used by Shokhi.
chunks.title: Selected practice recommendations for contraceptive use, fourth edition
chunks.source: WHO — Selected practice recommendations for contraceptive use, 4th edition (2025)

chunks.text: Advice depends on the pill type, how many hormonal pills were missed, where the person is in the pack, and whether unprotected sex happened. A safe digital helper should first identify the product and situation rather than give one rule for every pill. If the product or timing is unclear, the person should check the pack and speak with a pharmacist or family-planning worker.
chunks.title: Selected practice recommendations for contraceptive use, fourth edition
chunks.source: WHO — Selected practice recommendations for contraceptive use, 4th edition (2025)

chunks.text: Emergency contraception should be used as soon as possible after unprotected sex. Depending on the method, emergency contraception can be used within 5 days. The copper-bearing IUD is a highly effective option when provided by a qualified health worker. Emergency contraception does not protect against sexually transmitted infections and should not replace a regular method.
chunks.title: Selected practice recommendations for contraceptive use, fourth edition
chunks.source: WHO — Selected practice recommendations for contraceptive use, 4th edition (2025)

chunks.text: Counselling should respect the person's own decision and consider health history, breastfeeding, future pregnancy plans, preference for a method that needs little daily remembering, and protection from sexually transmitted infections. General information is not a prescription; a trained health worker can help choose and use a method safely.
chunks.title: Selected practice recommendations for contraceptive use, fourth edition
chunks.source: WHO — Selected practice recommendations for contraceptive use, 4th edition (2025)

chunks.text: Endometriosis is a chronic condition affecting roughly 10% of women and girls of reproductive age worldwide. Tissue similar to the lining of the uterus grows outside the uterus, causing inflammation and scarring.
chunks.title: Endometriosis

chunks.text: Many women have severe pain during menstruation and heavy bleeding. The condition often causes chronic pelvic pain that continues beyond the period, and pain during sex, bowel movements or urination. Up to half of women who struggle to conceive may have endometriosis. The pain can be debilitating enough to prevent work or school, and it is linked with fatigue, depression and anxiety.
chunks.title: Endometriosis

chunks.text: There is currently no cure, but symptoms can respond to pain-relief medicines (NSAIDs), hormonal contraceptives, and sometimes surgery. Diagnosis is often delayed by several years because symptoms vary and awareness is low. See a doctor for severe period pain, chronic pelvic pain, painful intercourse, or difficulty getting pregnant. Early diagnosis and care that combines medication, therapy and support can greatly improve quality of life.
chunks.title: Endometriosis
chunks.section: Diagnosis, treatment and when to seek care

chunks.text: The WHO Consolidated HIV guidelines on service delivery bring together WHO's recommendations on how HIV services should be organized, so that care is more people-centred, integrated and fair, and so more people can get tested, prevented and treated.
chunks.title: HIV services (prevention, testing and treatment)
chunks.source: WHO — Consolidated HIV guidelines: service delivery (2026)

chunks.text: The guidelines support delivering HIV testing, prevention and treatment in ways that fit people's lives — closer to the community, with less stigma, and joined up with other health services a woman may already use, such as antenatal (pregnancy) care, family planning and sexual-health services. Integrating HIV services with maternal and reproductive health helps reach women and prevent mother-to-child transmission.
chunks.title: HIV services (prevention, testing and treatment)
chunks.source: WHO — Consolidated HIV guidelines: service delivery (2026)

chunks.text: A central goal is to improve access, keep people in care over time (continuity of care), and reduce the steps and barriers between testing and treatment. HIV testing is confidential, and effective treatment allows a person living with HIV to stay healthy and prevents passing the virus to others. This is general information; a woman with concerns about HIV should speak with a health worker or visit a testing and treatment service, where support is confidential and non-judgmental.
chunks.title: HIV services (prevention, testing and treatment)
chunks.source: WHO — Consolidated HIV guidelines: service delivery (2026)

chunks.text: Menstruation is a natural monthly cycle, usually lasting 21 to 35 days. The lining of the uterus thickens, an egg is released around the middle of the cycle, and if pregnancy does not occur the lining is shed as menstrual blood. Most people menstruate without significant disruption to daily life; mild cramping, bloating and mood changes are common.
chunks.title: Menstrual health

chunks.text: More than two-thirds of people who menstruate experience menstrual pain, which can usually be eased with pain relief or heat. Nearly half experience heavy bleeding, which can lead to iron-deficiency anaemia. Symptoms that are unpredictable, severe or that disrupt daily life may point to conditions such as endometriosis, polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS), fibroids or a bleeding disorder.
chunks.title: Menstrual health

chunks.text: People who menstruate need clean water, private sanitation and clean absorbent materials (pads, cloth or reusable options), with safe disposal or washing. See a health worker for severe pain, very heavy bleeding, irregular cycles, or mood changes that disrupt work or school — these deserve a proper check.
chunks.title: Menstrual health
chunks.section: Hygiene and when to seek care

chunks.text:
Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) is a common hormonal condition in which the body has higher-than-normal levels of androgens. It affects an estimated 10–13% of women of reproductive age, and up to 70% of those affected remain undiagnosed.

Women with PCOS may have irregular or infrequent menstrual periods, difficulty getting pregnant, excess facial or body hair, hair loss, and acne. Symptoms vary a lot from person to person. PCOS is the most common cause of anovulation (no egg release) and a leading cause of infertility.
chunks.title: Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS)

chunks.text: PCOS is diagnosed by a health provider using menstrual history, blood tests for androgen levels, and sometimes an ultrasound of the ovaries — it cannot be confirmed from symptoms alone. Healthy lifestyle behaviours, including healthy eating and physical activity, are important for all women with PCOS. Medicines such as combined oral contraceptives can help regulate periods and reduce symptoms, and fertility treatment can help with conception. There is no cure, but symptoms can be managed. PCOS is also linked with a higher risk of insulin resistance, type 2 diabetes and heart disease, so regular check-ups help.
chunks.title: Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS)

chunks.text:
WHO's postnatal guideline brings together routine care recommendations for women and newborns during the first six weeks after birth. It describes a positive postnatal experience as one where women, babies, partners, parents, and caregivers receive understandable information, reassurance, and support in a respectful, person-centred way.

Postnatal care can include assessment of recovery, support for feeding, mental and emotional wellbeing, family-planning counselling, and help understanding newborn care. The exact schedule and services depend on local health-system guidance and the woman's or baby's needs.
chunks.title: WHO recommendations on maternal and newborn care for a positive postnatal experience
chunks.source: WHO — WHO recommendations on maternal and newborn care for a positive postnatal experience
chunks.section: The first six weeks after birth

chunks.text:
Shokhi can help a new mother prepare questions, notice changes in mood, ask for support, and discuss birth spacing with a health worker. It must not diagnose postpartum depression, infection, or newborn illness.

Heavy bleeding, fever, foul-smelling discharge, severe pain, breathing difficulty, or thoughts of self-harm require urgent help. Shokhi's deterministic safety rules take priority over educational retrieval.
chunks.title: WHO recommendations on maternal and newborn care for a positive postnatal experience
chunks.source: WHO — WHO recommendations on maternal and newborn care for a positive postnatal experience
chunks.section: How Shokhi should use this source

chunks.text: Postpregnancy family planning is the use of contraception after a pregnancy ends — either after childbirth (postpartum family planning) or after an abortion (post-abortion family planning) — by a woman who wants to avoid an unintended or closely spaced pregnancy. Spacing pregnancies gives the mother's body time to recover and is safer for both mother and baby.
chunks.title: Postpregnancy family planning
chunks.source: WHO — Scaling up postpregnancy family planning: practical guide (2025)

chunks.text: The time around childbirth and after an abortion is an important opportunity to offer a woman information and a method of her choice, because she is often in contact with health services. Access to postpregnancy family planning helps countries make progress toward the health goal (SDG 3) and gender-equality goal (SDG 5), and supports a woman's right to decide whether and when to have children.
chunks.title: Postpregnancy family planning
chunks.source: WHO — Scaling up postpregnancy family planning: practical guide (2025)

chunks.text: Good postpregnancy family-planning services offer counselling, a full range of methods, and respect for the woman's own decision, with attention to quality of care and gender equality. A woman can talk with a health worker before or soon after delivery about which method suits her, including methods that are safe while breastfeeding. This is general information; a doctor or family-planning worker can help her choose what is right for her personally.
